extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, journalism students, and feature journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and techniques for producing feature journalism that evokes emotion while maintaining journalistic objectivity; analyzes how Pulitzer-winning feature pieces use specific strategies to build an affective force. Useful for evaluating or composing long-form, narrative feature stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic ritual of objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity defined as the 'lack of favoritism toward one side or another, freedom of bias' and described by Tuchman (1972) as a 'strategic ritual' journalists follow to claim legitimacy and defend against criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists claim objectivity by citing procedures and formal elements of reporting (validation through documented practices). Tuchman outlines three factors that help define an objective fact—form, content, and interorganizational relationships—and recommends invoking such procedures to support claims of objectivity. Caveat: rigid adherence can 'trap' journalists and fail to capture journalistic judgement and the production process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors that support claims of objectivity (form, content, interorganizational relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuchman's three factors for defining an objective fact: form (the way a story is told), content (what the story is about), and interorganizational relationships (collaborations between entities that produce greater value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formal elements and documented procedures (quotations, documented sourcing practices, institutional procedures) to demonstrate objectivity. These factors are tools reporters use to 'claim objectivity' in the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic ritual of emotionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotionality is an institutionalized practice of narrating and infusing reporting with emotion; it is a strategic ritual distinct from expressing the journalist's own feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotionality should be methodized—outsourcing emotional labor to authorized non-journalists, using emotive language, dramatic tension, and detailed description to create affect. Note the alternative epistemology: some feature stories rely on narrative power rather than extensive quoting (Wahl-Jorgensen found only 6.2% of feature stories were based on direct/indirect quotes). The ritual is to present emotion objectively, not to foreground the reporter's personal emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not foreground the journalist's personal emotions; outsource emotional expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategic ritual of emotionality 'does not mean journalists should express their own emotions, but rather rely on an outsourcing of emotional labor to non-journalists' so emotions can be authoritatively described without contaminating objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sources whose emotions can be authoritatively described; use their reactions and recollections to convey affect while maintaining an objective stance. Anti-pattern: first-person self-indulgent emotionalizing by the reporter that undermines objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy as mediator between objectivity and emotionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Empathy—'the ability to understand and share feelings of another'—serves as the crucial link allowing journalists to understand and relay subjects' emotions while maintaining objectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empathy to adapt objective practices across subject matters (especially in feature pieces). Distinguish empathy from sympathy/compassion: empathy is an adaptive, cognitive tool for accurate relaying rather than emotional contagion. Employ empathy in reporting heavy or culturally complex topics; it enables authoritative, ethically grounded presentation of emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solidarity and humanizing techniques for marginalized communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Solidarity differs from empathy: while empathy may limit concern to 'worthy' individuals, solidarity expands concern to entire affected communities and is a technique for more inclusive humanization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When humanizing marginalized groups, aim for solidarity-based techniques that broaden scope rather than exceptionalize single subjects. Anti-pattern: humanizing that constrains concern to only exceptional individuals, which can misrepresent structural issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsourcing as a tactic to build affective force
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsourcing means referring to non-journalists (sources authorized to express emotions publicly) to present emotions objectively; journalists deliberately choose which information and quotes to include to build emotionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective for first-person accounts and stories of death/tragedy; examples include using family members, doctors, or other witnesses to supply emotional detail. Outsourcing can fill gaps the subject or journalist cannot objectively detail. Anti-pattern: in polarizing topics, naive outsourcing without accounting for all perspectives can contaminate objectivity; in such cases rely more on other strategies (humanizing repetition, contextual contrast).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanizing repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of short, declarative repetitions or repeated time stamps as a form of repetition with agency to humanize subjects and build emotional engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in features about niche ways of life or medical issues. Techniques include repeating phrases, mantras, or time stamps to create intimacy, suspense, or underscore a lived reality (examples: repeated weather lines for farming, repeated time cues in surgical narratives). Use repetition to show rather than tell; avoid mechanical or excessive repetition that feels manipulative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of time stamps and sensory detail to create immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition via time stamps and sensory detail (small quotidian details) humanizes subjects and immerses readers in scenes, increasing affective force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin or punctuate scenes with concrete times and sensory gestures (meals, sounds, objects) to make readers feel present. Example: opening lines that set precise times and small domestic details to humanize professionals or patients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce unfamiliar or unrelatable subjects into context by juxtaposing them with contrasting, relatable examples to evoke empathy and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short contrasts (e.g., 'he can do everything the rest of his class can do. Except see.') or juxtapose societal facts (e.g., fishermen deaths vs. whale protections) to make stakes clear. Combine with repetition and outsourcing for greater effect. Anti-pattern: false or unfair contrasts that oversimplify complex issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show-don't-tell and building affective force via selected detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow facts, quotes, reactions, and carefully chosen details to 'speak for themselves' to build intimacy and emotional investment rather than explicit emoting or exhaustive listing of grisly facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on narrative craft (showing reactions, using selective detail) to let readers draw conclusions and feel emotion. Example: emphasize surrounding characters' reactions instead of narrating every grim act. Avoid blunt exposition that tells the reader how to feel or overloads with gratuitous detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic-appropriate strategy selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of a feature story strongly determines which emotionality/objectivity techniques are appropriate and how they should be combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess topic sensitivity and polarizing potential: use outsourcing for personal tragedies, humanizing repetition for niche cultural immersion, contextual contrast when translating unfamiliar experiences for general audiences. Always consider whether a chosen tactic preserves objectivity given the topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical management of emotional labor and professionalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must manage their own emotions and the ethical implications of evoking emotion—methods include professionalism, process, and sometimes emotional silencing—to maintain accuracy and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare strategies for emotional labor when reporting trauma or genocide; maintain professional boundaries while employing empathy and solidarity. Journalistic responsibility includes accurately conveying subjects' emotions when 'invited in' and avoiding exploitation or sentimentalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of alternative epistemologies in feature storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Some features rely less on traditional objectivity-validation practices (e.g., extensive quoting) and more on the assumed epistemic authority of the journalist and the narrative's power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when narrative authority is being relied upon; still ensure ethical sourcing and verification. Be mindful that an over-reliance on assumed authority can obscure evidentiary support—balance narrative power with transparent sourcing when necessary.
